rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s command to purify His House is related to the mosque discussion.
rows.anchor: وطهر بيتي [الحج: 26]. وقال عليه السلام

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet said journeys should be undertaken only to three mosques; hadith authorities transmitted it, and Qurtubi says it was discussed earlier.
rows.anchor: لا تعمل المطي إلا إلى ثلاثة مساجد

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: Prayer in the Prophet’s mosque is better than a thousand elsewhere, except in the Sacred Mosque.
rows.anchor: صلاة في مسجدي هذا خير من ألف صلاة فيما سواه إلا المسجد الحرام

rows.speaker: ابن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-Arabi reports through a sound route that prayer in the Sacred Mosque is better than a hundred prayers in the Prophet’s mosque.
rows.anchor: قال ابن العربي: وقد روى من طريق لا بأس بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi affirms that further prayer-reward report as authentic through reliable transmitters, as explained in Ibrahim.
rows.anchor: قلت: هو صحيح بنقل العدل عن العدل حسب ما بيناه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mosques belong to and are honored by God, yet may be named after people for identification; attribution can reflect location or endowment.
rows.anchor: المساجد وإن كانت لله ملكا وتشريفا فإنها قد تنسب إلى غيره تعريفا

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A sound hadith describes the Prophet racing trained and untrained horses between named sites, illustrating local mosque naming.
rows.anchor: وفي صحيح الحديث: أن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم سابق بين الخيل التي أضمرت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The community agrees mosques, bridges, and cemeteries may be endowed, but jurists dispute endowing other property.
rows.anchor: ولا خلاف بين الأمة في تحبيس المساجد والقناطر والمقابر وإن اختلفوا في تحبيس غير ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Permitted mosque uses include dividing funds, sharing charity among the poor, detention, restraining captives, sleeping, housing the sick, neighbor access, and nonfalse poetry.
rows.anchor: فإنه تجوز القسمة فيها للأموال. ويجوز وضع الصدقات فيها على رسم الاشتراك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prohibition rebukes polytheists for invoking others alongside God in the Sacred Mosque.
rows.anchor: هذا توبيخ للمشركين في دعائهم مع الله غيره في المسجد الحرام

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says Jews and Christians practiced associationism in churches and synagogues, so believers must devote worship to God in every mosque and worship no idol there.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: كانت اليهود والنصارى إذا دخلوا كنائسهم وبيعهم أشركوا بالله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view reserves mosques for remembrance of God, not mockery, commerce, assemblies, passageways, or giving others a share in worship.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المعنى أفردوا المساجد لذكر الله، ولا تتخذوها هزوا ومتجرا ومجلسا

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet said to answer anyone announcing a lost item in a mosque with a prayer that it not be returned, since mosques were not built for that.
rows.anchor: من نشد ضالة في المسجد فقولوا لا ردها الله عليك فإن المساجد لم تبن لهذا

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A report through al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas says the Prophet entered right-foot first and prayed for release from the Fire, then exited left-foot first asking for abundant good and lasting blessing; no grading is stated.
rows.anchor: روى الضحاك عن ابن عباس عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening conjunction may be read with fatḥ as part of revelation to the Prophet, or with kasr as a new sentence.
rows.anchor: يجوز الفتح أي أوحى الله إليه أنه. ويجوز الكسر على الاستئناف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abd Allah is Muhammad, praying and reciting Quran at Batn Nakhlah, as recounted at the sura’s beginning.
rows.anchor: «عبد الله» هنا محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم حين كان يصلي ببطن نخلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb means that Muhammad worshipped God.
rows.anchor: أي يعبده. وقال ابن جريج: «يدعوه» أي قام إليهم داعيا

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj takes it to mean Muhammad stood calling the jinn to God.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جريج: «يدعوه» أي قام إليهم داعيا إلى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: الزبير بن العوام
rows.claim: Al-Zubayr says the jinn nearly piled on one another when they heard the Prophet reciting, eager to listen.
rows.anchor: قال الزبير بن العوام: هم الجن حين استمعوا القرآن من النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak says they crowded one upon another out of eagerness to hear.
rows.anchor: وقيل: كادوا يركبونه حرصا قاله الضحاك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says the jinn crowded together because they wanted to hear the remembrance.
rows.anchor: ابن عباس: رغبة في سماع الذكر

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: Burd reports from Makhul that seventy thousand jinn pledged allegiance to the Prophet that night and finished at daybreak; no grading is given.
rows.anchor: وروى برد عن مكحول: أن الجن بايعوا رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم في هذه الليلة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Another report from Ibn Abbas makes this the jinn’s account of Muhammad’s companions following him in bowing and prostration.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس أيضا: إن هذا من قول الجن لما رجعوا إلى قومهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says the polytheists crowded against one another in hostility toward the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وقيل: المعنى كاد المشركون يركبون بعضهم بعضا، حردا على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan, Qatada, and Ibn Zayd say humans and jinn massed against Muhammad at the valley to extinguish the light, but God granted victory and completed His light.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن وقتادة وابن زيد: يعني { لما قام عبد الله } محمد بالعدوة تلبدت الإنس والجن

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: Al-Tabari prefers that the Arabs nearly united against the Prophet to extinguish the light he brought.
rows.anchor: واختار الطبري أن يكون المعنى: كادت العرب يجتمعون على النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid glosses lubad as crowds, from things piling together; the root also describes compacted wool or anything stuck tightly together.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: قوله «لبدا» جماعات وهو من تلبد الشيء على الشيء أي تجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common reading has kasr on lam and fatḥ on ba; Mujahid, Ibn Muhaysin, and Hisham read damm on lam and fatḥ on ba, singular lubadah.
rows.anchor: وهي قراءة العامة. وضم اللام وفتح الباء، وهي قراءة مجاهد وابن محيصن وهشام عن أهل الشام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abu Haywah, Muhammad ibn al-Sumayqa, Abu al-Ashhab al-Uqayli, and al-Jahdari read damm on both letters; Hasan, Abu al-Aliyah, al-Araj, and al-Jahdari also read doubled ba with fatḥ.
rows.anchor: وبضم اللام والباء، وهي قراءة أبي حيوة ومحمد بن السميقع وأبي الأشهب العقيلي والجحدري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another gloss takes lubad as enduring, as in Luqman’s last vulture, Lubad; al-Nabigha’s poetry evokes its survival.
rows.anchor: وقيل: اللبد بضم اللام وفتح الباء الشيء الدائم ومنه قيل لنسر لقمان لبد

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayri records lubadan with both letters rounded as plural of lubayd, a small sack.
rows.anchor: القشيري: وقرىء «لبدا» بضم اللام والباء، وهو جمع لبيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lubad in “I destroyed abundant wealth” means plentiful; people are also called lubad when assembled, while al-labad can mean a homebody.
rows.anchor: وفي الصحاح: وقوله تعالى أهلكت مالا لبدا [البلد: 6] أي جما

rows.speaker: أبو عبيد
rows.claim: Abu Ubayd prefers a transmitted variant about a stay-at-home person; the cited verse praises good judgment and major undertakings.
rows.anchor: ويروى: اللبد. قال أبو عبيد: وهو أشبه. والبزلاء: الرأي الجيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arab lore says Luqman, sent by Ad to seek rain, chose seven vultures over seven ewes for long life; the last vulture was named Lubad.
rows.anchor: وتزعم العرب أن لقمان هو الذي بعثته عاد في وفدها إلى الحرم يستسقي لها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers have indicative قال; Hamza and Asim read imperative قل.
rows.anchor: وكذا قرأ أكثر القراء «قال» على ا لخبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Quraysh said Muhammad’s message made him everyone’s enemy and offered protection if he withdrew; this verse was revealed in response.
rows.anchor: وسبب نزولها أن كفار قريش قالوا له: إنك جئت بأمر عظيم وقد عاديت الناس كلهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad says he invokes only his Lord and associates no one with Him.
rows.anchor: وكذا قرأ أكثر القراء «قال» على ا لخبر

words: إني لا أملك لكم ضرا ولا رشدا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muhammad cannot ward off harm from his audience or bring them good.
rows.anchor: أي لا أقدر أن أدفع عنكم ضرا ولا أسوق لكم خيرا

words: إني لا أملك لكم ضرا ولا رشدا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes harm as disbelief and guidance as right guidance, leaving Muhammad only the duty to convey.
rows.anchor: وقيل: { لا أملك لكم ضرا } أي كفرا { ولا رشدا } أي هدى

words: إني لا أملك لكم ضرا ولا رشدا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other glosses take harm as punishment and guidance as bliss, or respectively death and life.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الضر: العذاب، والرشد النعيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Leave me” is a threat and warning.
rows.anchor: ذرني } أي دعني وهي كلمة وعيد وتهديد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the ordinary reading, wahidan is circumstantial for the omitted object: God created him alone, with no wealth or children, then bestowed gifts.
rows.anchor: ف «وحيدا» على هذا حال من ضمير المفعول المحذوف، أي خلقته وحده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentators identify the man as al-Walid ibn al-Mughira al-Makhzumi, singled out for ingratitude and harming the Messenger.
rows.anchor: والمفسرون على أنه الوليد بن المغيرة المخزومي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says al-Walid boasted he was the unique son of a unique father, with no Arab equal; God repeats the boast without endorsing it.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: كان الوليد يقول: أنا الوحيد بن الوحيد

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid takes the phrase as God’s challenge to deal with al-Walid alone, sufficient to avenge him.
rows.anchor: أحدهما: ذرني وحدي معه فأنا أجزيك في الانتقام منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading makes wahidan describe God as sole creator, able to destroy al-Walid without a helper.
rows.anchor: والثاني: أني انفردت بخلقه ولم يشركني فيه أحد، فأنا أهلكه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says al-Walid began alone in his mother’s womb, without wealth or child, before God enriched him.
rows.anchor: والأول قول مجاهد، أي خلقته وحيدا في بطن أمه لا مال له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation says he will be resurrected alone just as created alone.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أراد بذلك ليدله على أنه يبعث وحيدا كما خلق وحيدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another gloss calls al-Walid one without a known father; Qurtubi links it to his description in 68:13.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الوحيد الذي لا يعرف أبوه، وكان الوليد معروفا بأنه دعي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas lists camels, horses, livestock, gardens, and male and female slaves between Mecca and Taif.
rows.anchor: وهو ما كان للوليد بين مكة والطائف من الإبل والحجور والنعم والجنان

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, and Ibn Abbas give annual income of one thousand dinars.
rows.anchor: غلة ألف دينار قاله سعيد بن جبير وابن عباس أيضا

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatada estimates six thousand dinars; Sufyan al-Thawri and Qatada give four thousand, and Sufyan also gives one million.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: ستة آلاف دينار

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says al-Walid owned an orchard whose produce never ceased in winter or summer.
rows.anchor: مقاتل: كان له بستان لا ينقطع خيره شتاء ولا صيفا

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: Umar interprets the wealth as monthly income, month after month.
rows.anchor: وقال عمر رضي الله عنه: { وجعلت له مالا ممدودا } غلة شهر بشهر

rows.speaker: النعمان بن سالم
rows.claim: Nuʿman ibn Salim says it means cultivated land.
rows.anchor: النعمان بن سالم: أرضا يزرع فيها

rows.speaker: القشيري
rows.claim: Al-Qushayri prefers recurring income such as crops, livestock, and trade.
rows.anchor: القشيري: والأظهر أنه إشارة إلى ما لا ينقطع رزقه، بل يتوالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sons are present with al-Walid and do not leave while he conducts his affairs.
rows.anchor: أي حضورا لا يغيبون عنه في تصرف

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid and Qatada say ten sons; al-Suddi and al-Dahhak say twelve, including seven born in Mecca and five in Taif; Saʿid says thirteen.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد وقتادة: كانوا عشرة

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil says seven sons, all male, and three converted: Khalid, Hisham, and al-Walid ibn al-Walid; their father’s wealth and children declined until he died.
rows.anchor: مقاتل: كانوا سبعة كلهم رجال، أسلم منهم ثلاثة: خالد وهشام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God spread ease and luxury around al-Walid so he could live secure and comfortable in his town, acting at discretion.
rows.anchor: أي بسطت له في العيش بسطا، حتى أقام ببلدته مطمئنا مترفها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Arabic, tamhid means preparing and making something ready, as when preparing a child’s bed.
rows.anchor: والتمهيد عند العرب: التوطئة والتهيئة ومنه مهد الصبي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas and Mujahid say the preparation was ample territory between Yemen and Syria.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: { ومهدت له تمهيدا } أي وسعت له ما بين اليمن والشام

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid also says it means wealth piled on wealth, like bedding.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد أيضا في { ومهدت له تمهيدا } أنه المال بعضه فوق بعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After all those gifts, al-Walid hoped God would increase his wealth and children.
rows.anchor: أي ثم إن الوليد يطمع بعد هذا كله أن أزيده في المال والولد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The direct sense is God will not increase his gifts because al-Walid disbelieves in His favors.
rows.anchor: أي ليس يكون ذلك مع كفره بالنعم

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan and others say al-Walid hoped to enter Paradise, claiming that if Muhammad were truthful Paradise was created for him; God rejects this.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن وغيره: أي ثم يطمع أن أدخله الجنة، وكان الوليد يقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi says al-Walid’s wealth and children kept diminishing until he died.
rows.anchor: فلم يزل يرى النقصان في ماله وولده حتى هلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thumma is exclamatory, not sequential, expressing astonishment; Qurtubi links it to 6:1 and an analogy of giving much only to be treated harshly.
rows.anchor: و «ثم» في قوله تعالى: { ثم يطمع } ليست بثم التي للنسق ولكنها تعجيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says al-Walid hoped provision would remain among his descendants, thinking Muhammad’s memory would end at his death.
rows.anchor: وقيل يطمع أن أترك ذلك في عقبه وذلك أنه كان يقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further interpretation says al-Walid hoped God would support him despite disbelief.
rows.anchor: وقيل: أي ثم يطمع أن أنصره على كفره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kalla may close hope of increase and connect to preceding words, or mean “indeed” and begin the next statement.
rows.anchor: وقيل: { كلا } بمعنى حقا ويكون ابتداء

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Al-Walid is obstinate toward Muhammad and revelation; Mujahid glosses ʿanid as rejecting known truth.
rows.anchor: يقال: عاند فهو عنيد مثل جالس فهو جليس قاله مجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAnid opposes or rejects known truth; the root describes a camel straying from its path.
rows.anchor: وعند يعند بالكسر أي خالف ورد الحق وهو يعرفه فهو عنيد وعاند

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God will put the threatened person into Saqar to suffer its heat.
rows.anchor: أي سأدخله سقر كي يصلى حرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saqar is named from the sun melting, scorching, and burning skin; it is indeclinable because definite and feminine.
rows.anchor: وإنما سميت سقر من سقرته الشمس: إذا أذابته ولوحته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas identifies Saqar as the sixth level of Hell.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: هي الطبق السادس من جهنم

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: Abu Hurayra reports Moses asking God which servant was poorest; God replied, the inhabitant of Saqar. Al-Thaʿlabi gives no grading.
rows.anchor: وروى أبو هريرة: أن رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم قال:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question intensifies Saqar’s description and magnifies it.
rows.anchor: هذه مبالغة في وصفها أي وما أعلمك أي شيء هي؟ وهي كلمة تعظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saqar leaves no bone, flesh, or blood unburned; repetition emphasizes totality.
rows.anchor: أي لا تترك لهم عظما ولا لحما ولا دما إلا أحرقته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says nothing remains, then they are recreated and burned again continually.
rows.anchor: وقيل: لا تبقي منهم شيئا، ثم يعادون خلقا جديدا، فلا تذر

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid says it leaves no one alive or dead, burning them whenever renewed.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد: لا تبقي من فيها حيا ولا تذره ميتا

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says it leaves no flesh and no bone.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: لا تبقي لهم لحما ولا تذر لهم عظما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lawwaha means changing or disfiguring, from the verb meaning to change.
rows.anchor: أي مغيرة، من لاحه إذا غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common nominative makes lawwaha an adjective of Saqar; Atiyya al-Awfi, Nasr ibn Asim, and Isa ibn Umar read accusative as emphatic specification.
rows.anchor: وقراءة العامة «لواحة» بالرفع نعت ل «سقر»

rows.speaker: أبو رزين
rows.claim: Abu Razin says its flame scorches faces, leaving them blacker than night; Mujahid also transmits this.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو رزين: تلفح وجوههم لفحة تدعها أشد سوادا من الليل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Arabic usage says cold, heat, illness, and grief change a person; poetry supports this sense of laaha.
rows.anchor: والعرب تقول: لاحه البرد والحر والسقم والحزن: إذا غيره

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says Saqar is visible to people from five hundred years away.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: { لواحة } أي تلوح للبشر من مسيرة خمسمائة عام

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan and Ibn Kaysan say Hell appears until people see it plainly.
rows.anchor: الحسن وابن كيسان: تلوح لهم جهنم حتى يروها عيانا

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash derives the word from thirst: Saqar makes its inhabitants thirsty; poetry uses lawh for severe thirst.
rows.anchor: والمعنى أنها معطشة للبشر أي لأهلها قاله الأخفش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi connects Hell’s appearance with its being brought into view for the wayward in 26:91.
rows.anchor: وبرزت الجحيم للغاوين [الشعراء: 91]

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: Al-Akhfash and most exegetes take bashar as the human inhabitants of Hell.
rows.anchor: أحدهما أنه الإنس من أهل النار قاله الأخفش والأكثرون

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid and Qatada take bashar as human skin, plural abshar; Ibn Abbas’s distant-visible gloss instead means people because it refers to shining.
rows.anchor: الثاني أنه جمع بشرة، وهي جلدة الإنسان الظاهرة قاله مجاهد وقتادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nineteen angels are stationed over Saqar to cast its inhabitants into it.
rows.anchor: أي على سقر تسعة عشر من الملائكة يلقون فيها أهلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say nineteen guard the whole Fire, Malik plus eighteen; others suggest nineteen chiefs, while most exegetes take them as individual angels.
rows.anchor: ثم قيل: على جملة النار تسعة عشر من الملائكة هم خزنتها مالك

rows.speaker: الثعلبي
rows.claim: Al-Thaʿlabi says nineteen is plausible: one angel takes all souls, so nineteen can torment part of creation.
rows.anchor: الثعلبي: ولا ينكر هذا، فإذا كان ملك واحد يقبض أرواح جميع الخلائق

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj reports the Prophet describing the keepers as fearsome, with flashing eyes, tong-like mouths, great strength, and power to drive people and mountains into the Fire; no grading stated.
rows.anchor: نعت النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم خزنة جهنم فقال: «فكأن أعينهم البرق

rows.speaker: أبو العوام
rows.claim: A report via Ibn al-Mubarak from a Tamimi man says each keeper bears a two-pronged mace whose blow sends seventy thousand into Hell.
rows.anchor: عن رجل من بني تميم قال: كنا عند أبي العوام، فقرأ هذه الآية

rows.speaker: عمرو بن دينار
rows.claim: Amr ibn Dinar says each keeper can push more people into Hell at once than Rabiʿa and Mudar.
rows.anchor: وعن عمرو بن دينار: كل واحد منهم يدفع بالدفعة الواحدة في جهنم

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: Jabir reports Jews asking the Companions the keepers’ number; Muhammad answers nineteen and explains Paradise’s soil as flour for bread. Al-Tirmidhi calls it gharīb, known only through Mujalid and al-Shaʿbi.
rows.anchor: خرج الترمذي عن جابر بن عبد الله قال:

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A report through Ibn Wahb and Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd says a keeper’s shoulders are as far apart as east and west.
rows.anchor: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم في خزنة جهنم:

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas says a keeper’s shoulders are a year’s journey apart and one mace strike can drive seventy thousand to Hell’s bottom.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: ما بين منكبي الواحد منهم مسيرة سنة، وقوة الواحد منهم أن يضرب بالمقمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurtubi prefers that the nineteen are chiefs, whose full number is beyond human reckoning, as 74:31 says.
rows.anchor: قلت: والصحيح إن شاء الله أن هؤلاء التسعة عشر، هم الرؤساء والنقباء، وأما جملتهم

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: An authenticated report from Ibn Masud says Hell will be brought with seventy thousand reins, each drawn by seventy thousand angels.
rows.anchor: وقد ثبت في الصحيح عن عبد الله بن مسعود قال: قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم:

rows.speaker: أبو جهل
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Qatada, and al-Dahhak report Abu Jahl mocking the nineteen keepers and challenging Quraysh to overpower them.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس وقتادة والضحاك: لما نزل: { عليها تسعة عشر } قال أبو جهل لقريش

rows.speaker: أبو الأسود بن كلدة
rows.claim: Al-Suddi says Abu al-Aswad mocked handling ten angels with one shoulder and nine with the other; another version has al-Harith ibn Kalda claiming to handle seventeen.
rows.anchor: قال السدي: فقال أبو الأسود بن كلدة الجمحي: لا يهولنكم التسعة عشر

rows.speaker: أبو جهل
rows.claim: Another report says Abu Jahl asked whether one hundred could not overpower each angel and escape the Fire.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إن أبا جهل قال أفيعجز كل مائة منكم أن يبطشوا بواحد منهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God made the keepers angels rather than men so the damned would not try to overpower them.
rows.anchor: أي لم نجعلهم رجالا فتتعاطون مغالبتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says angels differ from the humans and jinn they punish, feel no kinship-based pity, and are devoted to God and strongest in force.
rows.anchor: وقيل: جعلهم ملائكة لأنهم خلاف جنس المعذبين من الجن والإنس، فلا يأخذهم ما يأخذ المجانس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fitna means a trial or affliction.
rows.anchor: أي بلية. وروي عن ابن عباس من غير وجه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas glosses the number as deviation for disbelievers, especially Abu Jahl and associates.
rows.anchor: وروي عن ابن عباس من غير وجه قال: ضلالة للذين كفروا، يريد أبا جهل وذويه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another gloss takes fitna as punishment, matching people tried in the Fire in 51:13–14.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إلا عذابا، كما قال تعالى:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common form is tisʿata ʿashara; Abu Jaʿfar and Talha read the first word with a still ʿayn.
rows.anchor: وفي «تسعة عشر» سبع قراءات: قراءة العامة «تسعة عشر».

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas is reported with damm on the hāʾ.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس «تسعة عشر» بضم الهاء

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas has two reported forms of tisʿata wa-ʿashr; al-Mahdawi explains the unjoined form as original before compounding, with nunation omitted in common usage.
rows.anchor: وعن أنس بن مالك «تسعة وعشر» وعنه أيضا «تسعة وعشر»

rows.speaker: أنس بن مالك
rows.claim: Anas is also reported to read tisʿata aʿshur; al-Mahdawi calls it unknown and Abu Hatim rejects it, while al-Zamakhshari analyzes it as plural of ʿashir.
rows.anchor: وعنه أيضا «تسعة أعشر» ذكرها المهدوي وقال: من قرأ

rows.speaker: المهدوي
rows.claim: Al-Mahdawi says stilling ʿayn avoids successive vowels; separated forms preserve earlier construction and a pause on rāʾ.
rows.anchor: وقال: من قرأ «تسعة عشر» أسكن العين لتوالي الحركات

rows.speaker: أبو حاتم
rows.claim: Abu Hatim rejects waw forms because they depend on unsupported aʿshur, with waw substituted for hamza, which grammarians reject.
rows.anchor: وكذلك «تسعة وعشر» لأنها محمولة على «تسعة أعشر» والواو بدل من الهمزة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas, Qatada, al-Dahhak, Mujahid, and others say the count confirms Torah and Gospel; it may refer to believing scripturalists like Abd Allah ibn Salam or all of them.
rows.anchor: قاله ابن عباس وقتادة والضحاك ومجاهد وغيرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers increase in faith by trusting scripture and affirming the number of Hell’s keepers.
rows.anchor: آمنوا، ثم ازدادوا إيمانا لتصديقهم بعدد خزنة جهنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Neither the People of the Book nor Muhammad’s believers doubt the number of Hell’s keepers.
rows.anchor: أي ولا يشك { الذين أوتوا الكتاب } أي أعطوا الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentators identify diseased hearts as Medinan hypocrites who arose after the Hijra; Mecca had none.
rows.anchor: أي في صدورهم شك ونفاق من منافقي أهل المدينة، الذين ينجمون في مستقبل الزمان

rows.speaker: الحسين بن الفضل
rows.claim: Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl says the Meccan sura has no hypocrites, so disease means disagreement or doubt and disbelievers are Arab polytheists.
rows.anchor: قال الحسين بن الفضل: السورة مكية ولم يكن بمكة نفاق فالمرض في هذه الآية الخلاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most commentators take disbelievers as Jews and Christians; another view makes disease doubt among Meccans, some certain Muhammad lied.
rows.anchor: ماذآ أراد الله بهذا مثلا

rows.speaker: الليث
rows.claim: Al-Layth says mathal can mean a report; 13:35’s likeness of Paradise means its account and description.
rows.anchor: قال الليث: المثل الحديث ومنه: «مثل الجنة التي وعد المتقون» أي حديثها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God disgraces Abu Jahl’s deniers while guiding Muhammad’s companions; alternatively, He misleads from Paradise or guides to it.
rows.anchor: أبا جهل وأصحابه المنكرين لخزنة جهنم

words: وَمَا يَعْلَمُ جُنُودَ رَبِّكَ إِلَّا هُوَ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only God knows the number of angels created to punish Hell’s people, answering Abu Jahl’s taunt that Muhammad had only nineteen forces.
rows.anchor: أي وما يدري عدد ملائكة ربك الذين خلقهم لتعذيب أهل النار «إلا هو»

words: وَمَا يَعْلَمُ جُنُودَ رَبِّكَ إِلَّا هُوَ
rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reports at Hunayn that Gabriel sat with the Prophet when an unfamiliar angel brought a command; Gabriel said not every angel of God was known to him.
rows.anchor: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم كان يقسم غنائم حنين، فأتاه جبريل

words: وَمَا يَعْلَمُ جُنُودَ رَبِّكَ إِلَّا هُوَ
rows.speaker: الأوزاعي
rows.claim: Al-Awzaʿi transmits Moses asking who is in heaven and how many angels; God says twelve tribes, each as numerous as dust.
rows.anchor: وقال الأوزاعي: قال موسى: «يا رب من في السماء؟ قال ملائكتي

words: وَمَا يَعْلَمُ جُنُودَ رَبِّكَ إِلَّا هُوَ
rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet says the sky groans rightly: each four-finger space contains an angel prostrating; al-Tirmidhi transmits it.
rows.anchor: وفي الترمذي عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view takes it as the signs, proofs, and Quran, reminders for humanity.
rows.anchor: يعني الدلائل والحجج والقرآن. وقيل: { وما هي }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes it as Saqar, an admonition for humanity.
rows.anchor: أي وما هذه النار التي هي سقر

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj says worldly fire reminds of the Fire of the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: وقيل: نار الدنيا تذكرة لنار الآخرة. قاله الزجاج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view makes the keepers’ number a reminder of God’s power and lack of need for helpers; the pronoun refers to the nearest antecedent, the troops.
rows.anchor: وأنه لا يحتاج إلى أعوان وأنصار
